subject: anaesthesia
title: ICP, cerebral protection and aneurysm surgery

steps.tx: The skull holds brain, blood and cerebrospinal fluid in a fixed volume, so any added mass raises **intracranial pressure** as described by the **Monro-Kellie** doctrine. The team keeps **cerebral perfusion pressure** near 60 to 70 and treats a blown pupil or the Cushing response as herniation. Drainage, head elevation and osmotic therapy buy time quickly.
steps.say: The skull holds the brain, blood and spinal fluid inside a fixed and rigid space. Any extra swelling or blood raises the pressure inside that closed space. Doctors protect the blood flow to the brain and keep its perfusion pressure near the target range. A blown pupil with slow pulse and high blood pressure can warn the team about dangerous herniation.

steps.tx: This scan shows **midline shift** with the uncus pushing inward as **uncal herniation**, and the basal cisterns look effaced. The inset shows an **external ventricular drain** catheter placed inside the ventricle to drain fluid. These findings matter because herniation can compress the brainstem and kill the patient quickly. Recognising this pattern helps you choose urgent drainage and osmotic treatment in the exam.
steps.say: The scan shows the midline pushed away from its normal central position. One inner part of the temporal lobe has slipped inward and threatens the brainstem below. The fluid spaces around the brainstem look squeezed and almost disappear on the scan. The small inset shows a drain that removes spinal fluid from the ventricle. This picture teaches urgent recognition because delayed treatment can cause permanent brain injury.

steps.tx: A ruptured **aneurysm** causes **subarachnoid haemorrhage** with thunderclap headache and neck stiffness, and grading helps to predict the outcome. An anterior communicating aneurysm may affect vision fields, while a posterior one may injure the third nerve. The surgeon secures the neck by **clipping** or the radiologist fills the sac by coiling, as this figure compares. Securing the aneurysm early prevents a fatal rebleed.
steps.say: The figure compares two ways of securing a ruptured aneurysm inside the brain. One approach will place a metal clip across the neck through an open operation. The other approach will fill the sac with coils that reach it through a blood vessel. Both methods aim to stop blood from entering the weak sac again. Early treatment matters because a second bleed often causes severe harm.

vis.alt: Diagram showing cerebral aneurysm, surgical clipping, and endovascular coiling.
vis.caption: Aneurysm treatment: clipping and coiling

steps.tx: Cerebral protection aims to lower the metabolic demand of the injured brain while the team maintains oxygen and glucose delivery. **Propofol** reduces cerebral metabolic rate, and **burst suppression** on the electroencephalogram shows a deeply quiet brain. The team avoids hyperglycaemia, treats seizures promptly and uses **hypothermia** only in selected cases. Careful positioning also protects the brain during the operation.
steps.say: Doctors protect the injured brain by reducing how much oxygen the brain tissue needs. Deep anaesthesia can quiet the electrical activity until the tracing shows burst suppression. The team also controls blood sugar carefully and treats any seizure without delay. Selected patients may receive controlled cooling under close monitoring in intensive care. Good positioning and smooth anaesthesia further reduce stress on the brain.

steps.tx: Surgery in the **posterior fossa** needs close monitoring because vital cranial nerves lie very near the operative field. The prone position can allow venous air entry, and nitrous oxide can expand trapped air as **pneumocephalus**. Pituitary surgery through the nose may cause a spinal fluid leak or **diabetes insipidus** after operation. A smooth emergence without coughing helps to prevent bleeding inside the head.
steps.say: The back part of the skull is home to the brainstem and many important cranial nerves. Surgeons monitor those nerves closely because even a small injury can affect swallowing or eye movement. Air trapped inside the skull can expand when certain anaesthetic gases are used. Surgery near the pituitary gland can disturb water balance and cause excessive urine output. A calm wake up without coughing reduces the risk of fresh bleeding.
